rituals.name: BRANCH DESCENT
rituals.plain:
Two rules, one thought. Certainty has to follow instructions too.
Take your current conclusion. Reduce a supported piece to its smallest fact. For a guess, name three plausible alternatives plus UNKNOWN. Follow only the branch that still matters most.
Shrink facts. Give guesses alternatives.
Stop at one statement you could check, ask about, notice or act on.

If unsure, choose UNKNOWN.

rituals.name: DUAL-CADENCE CHECK

One cadence checks meaning; the other checks action.
Notice which question appears less often but changes the direction more.

rituals.name: REVERSIBILITY TEST
rituals.plain:
Double it, then halve it. Your estimate went sightseeing.
Choose the number your mind is implying—chance, severity, or importance. Double it in imagination, then halve that doubled value so you return to the starting number.
The outside facts can't change during the round.
Compare the final feeling with the original. If the number is identical but the felt certainty is not, mark the mismatch.

rituals.name: CAUSE ROTATOR
rituals.plain:
Rotate the pieces of the story. The usual arrangement isn't sacred.
Reduce the thought to EVENT / MEANING / PREDICTION. Read it once in the normal order, then rotate to MEANING / PREDICTION / EVENT, then PREDICTION / EVENT / MEANING.
Keep the three pieces identical; change only their order.
Find the order in which the story starts sounding obviously strange.

rituals.name: SIGNAL GATE
rituals.plain:
Let the outside world cue the next count. Your thoughts don't own the schedule.
Hold the issue lightly. Listen for one real sound. After hearing it, allow exactly one sentence of thinking. Then stop and wait for a different sound before another sentence is allowed.
No new analysis until a new sound has been heard.
If the mind tries to continue without a sound, count that as an unsignalled continuation and don't follow it.

rituals.name: URGENCY LATENCY
rituals.plain:
Same thought, wider gaps. They don't need to tailgate.
Let the thought say itself once. Before the next repetition, leave a short blank. Make the next blank longer, then longer again, while refusing to add reassurance or new content.
The sentence stays the same; only the waiting time grows.
Notice whether urgency fades before the wording changes.

rituals.name: RANDOM ANCHOR

Let the thought begin its usual sequence. At an unplanned moment, choose any digit from 0–9 without pattern and hold only that digit for two beats.

When you release the digit, watch whether the chain continues automatically or has to rebuild its next step.

rituals.name: TIME DIAL
rituals.plain:
Put each worry where it belongs on the clock. Not everything is due at noon.
Imagine a clock face with NOW at 12. Place each claim from the thought around the dial according to when it could genuinely happen—minutes, hours, days, weeks, or unknown.
Nothing future is allowed to sit at NOW.
Look at 12 again and keep only what truly belongs there.

rituals.name: ACTION GHOST
rituals.plain:
Imagine the movement without doing it. The action can stay backstage.
When the urge suggests doing something, imagine the exact finger or hand rhythm that would begin the action, but keep your body still. Let the motor pattern complete only in imagination.
Imagined movement is allowed; actual movement is not required.
After the imagined rhythm ends, choose a different physical action with your real body.

Same words, unexpected beat. The sentence has learned to dance.
Say the thought silently once normally. Repeat it several times, each time stressing a different word—including one that would never normally receive emphasis.
Every word stays; only the stressed word changes.
Find the emphasis that changes the implied accusation, certainty, or responsibility most.

rituals.name: BREATH INDEPENDENCE
rituals.plain:
Your breathing doesn't need a supervisor for this count. The breath manager can resign.
Name three neutral things you can see, one after another, at whatever pace they appear. Let breathing happen on its own schedule while the naming continues.
Don't match the task to breathing.
If you notice yourself waiting for an inhale or exhale before the next item, deliberately continue at a different point in the breath cycle.

rituals.name: CERTAINTY DECAY
rituals.plain:
Move the estimate down in equal steps. Let's find its negotiating voice.
Take the certainty number your mind is implying. Subtract the same small amount three times—such as 7 points each time—while keeping all outside information unchanged.
No new reassuring facts may be added.
Notice the first step that suddenly feels 'too low' and ask what evidence created that boundary.

rituals.name: PRO-CON OSCILLATOR

Notice which side runs out of distinct evidence first.

rituals.name: REPETITION COLLAPSE
rituals.plain:
A hundred repeats can still be one claim. Loud isn't a voting system.
Imagine every recurrence of the same thought as identical dots. Merge all the dots into one single dot and place the number of repeats beside it.
Repeated copies don't get extra content.
Look at the one dot first, then the count. Ask which one was creating the sense of importance.

rituals.name: INTERPRETATION MATRIX
rituals.plain:
Can the same facts fit another arrangement? Your first story isn't royalty.
Imagine three observations as rows and three plausible interpretations as columns. Fill the matrix so each row and column gets one distinct fit instead of letting one story explain everything.
No explanation may be reused just to fill every cue.
Notice which observation refuses to belong exclusively to your original interpretation.

rituals.name: OPPORTUNITY-COST SHADOW
rituals.plain:
Choosing this means leaving something else. The hidden cost wants a seat.
Suppose you spend Saturday morning on Option A. Name the single best thing you would otherwise do with those same hours and place it beside A as the opportunity cost.
Use one scarce resource such as time or money.
Don't list every alternative—only the best forgone one.

rituals.name: PRIORITY LADDER
rituals.plain:
Which criterion actually matters first? The loudest option can wait.
Rank three criteria 1–3. Compare options only on criterion 1; use criterion 2 only if tied, then criterion 3 only if still tied.
Lower criteria can't override a clear win on a higher criterion.
Don't average criteria into one score.

rituals.plain:

rituals.name: CUE PROMISE
rituals.plain:
Let one real cue carry the reminder. Your memory can stop nagging.
Choose one future cue—opening a door, seeing a name, reaching a time—and pair it with one exact action. Then deliberately think about something unrelated for a short moment.
The cue must be specific enough to appear in the real world.
Bring back only the cue and see whether the action returns without replaying the original worry.

rituals.name: LOOP TWO-BACK
rituals.plain:
Did that thought appear two turns ago? Some repeats wear disguises.
Follow the next few thought steps as A, B, C, D. Each time a new one arrives, compare its mental job with the thought two positions back.
Compare mental jobs, not exact wording.
If A and C match in function, mark a hidden loop even if B made the stream feel new.

Every fair coin flip remains independent.
Don't average across the six flips; judge only the next one.

rituals.name: ONE-MOVE REPAIR
rituals.plain:
One move to repair the equation. No demolishing the whole house.
Find the smallest assumption or relationship that, if altered once, would make the conclusion fit the known facts better. Move only that one piece.
Just one mental piece may change; everything else is locked.
If you need a second repair, restore the first and try a different single move instead.

rituals.name: ASSUMPTION HUB

List a few conclusions inside the thought and the assumptions each one depends on. Count how many direct links point to each assumption.
Count direct dependencies only; don't count the same path twice.
Temporarily set the highest-degree assumption to UNKNOWN and watch how many conclusions lose support.

rituals.name: SUPPORT RATIO
rituals.plain:
Compare the two stories as fractions. Vague ratings can take leave.
For option A, count distinct supports and distinct assumptions. Do the same for B. Compare A-support × B-assumptions against B-support × A-assumptions.
Evidence and assumptions stay separate in each ratio.
Notice whether the option that felt stronger actually has the better support-to-assumption ratio.

rituals.name: CERTAINTY LOCK
rituals.plain:
Your conclusion needs a three-part combination. Confidence isn't the master key.
Ask what three distinct things would need to be true for the conclusion to deserve high certainty. Treat them as three lock positions and test each against what you actually know.
Each condition must add different information.
If one condition is unknown, leave that digit blank instead of guessing it.

rituals.name: EXPLANATION SIEVE
rituals.plain:
Which explanations are genuinely different? Some are wearing each other's coats.
List the possible causes your mind is generating. For each one, test whether it's merely a more elaborate version of another candidate using the same facts.
A complicated explanation can't stay if a simpler candidate already accounts for the same observations.
Remove every explanation that adds complexity without adding a new prediction.

rituals.name: PRIORITY TOURNAMENT

Only two concerns are compared at a time.
The final winner receives the next action; the other three are not re-litigated this round.

rituals.name: DOUBLE-STANDARD MATRIX
rituals.plain:
Would you use this rule in a similar case? Double standards need an introduction.
Find a comparable case where you know what you would conclude. State the rule connecting that case to its conclusion. Apply the same rule to your current situation.
The relationship must stay constant when the person or situation changes.
If the rule suddenly changes for you, name exactly what new fact justifies the exception.

Compare options pairwise using the fixed voter rankings.

rituals.name: PAST-COST CUT
rituals.plain:
Yesterday's effort wants a vote. Sunk cost isn't on the committee.
Imagine you spent two hours on a project that now looks unhelpful. Compare CONTINUE and STOP using only what each option costs and gives from this moment forward.
Past time or money can't be counted as a future benefit.
Every reason beginning with 'but I've already...' is disqualified.

rituals.name: LOCATION TRACE
rituals.plain:
Give the replay locations instead of sentences. Your thoughts can change furniture.
Take three or four elements from the repeating thought and place each at a different imagined location around you. Then recall only the sequence of locations.
Store position, not wording.
Try to reconstruct the original wording from the spatial path and notice where it becomes less automatic.

rituals.name: GOAL-GRADIENT PULL
rituals.plain:
Bring the next finish line closer. Motivation likes a visible doorstep.
Imagine a ten-step task where the next step is the same simple action. First picture yourself at step 1 of 10; then picture yourself at step 9 of 10. Compare the pull to perform that next action.
The next required action is unchanged across the two rounds.
Don't change reward, difficulty or time—only apparent progress.

rituals.name: BRANCH INVARIANT

Remove a few possibilities under one clear rule. The pile can lose some luggage.
Count the distinct future branches your mind is actively running. Remove one to three low-value branches and aim to leave a small stable set that you could actually compare.
Remove only a few branches at a time; don't solve each one.
If new branches appear, remove only enough to return to the chosen stable size.

rituals.name: CONFLICT COLOURS

Which problems actually compete for the same space? The pile isn't one creature.
Think of each active concern as a node. Draw a mental link only where two concerns compete for the same resource or decision. Assign colours so linked concerns never share one.
Only genuinely conflicting concerns need different colours.
Count the minimum colours needed rather than the number of concerns.

rituals.name: TEMPTATION BUNDLE
rituals.plain:
Pair one pleasant thing with one avoided task. Your task gets a better date.
Choose a harmless treat such as a favourite playlist. Mentally set the rule: playlist ON only while doing the first ten minutes of the avoided task; playlist OFF when the task stops.
The pleasant item is available only while doing the target task.
Don't give yourself the reward in advance.

rituals.name: SUBJECTIVE MIDPOINT
rituals.plain:
Where did halfway feel like it was? Your inner clock has opinions.
Let the thought or body alarm be present for a short manageable interval. Mark internally when you believe half the interval has passed.
No counting or breath timing.
After the interval ends, compare whether the first half felt longer or shorter than the second.

rituals.name: FORECAST DRIFT
rituals.plain:
Run fact and forecast side by side. Prediction may wander off script.
Imagine two tracks beginning together: WHAT IS KNOWN and WHAT I EXPECT NEXT. Advance them one step at a time.
A prediction step needs a matching evidence step to stay in sync.
Mark the first moment the forecast moves ahead while the known-facts track has nothing new.

rituals.name: CHANGE-OF-CHANGE
rituals.plain:
Is the problem accelerating, or staying unpleasant? Your forecast may be adding rocket fuel.
Give the last four moments rough intensity numbers. Subtract adjacent values to get three changes, then compare those changes with one another.
Judge changes between moments, not the moments alone.
If the second differences are near zero, label the pattern STEADY rather than ACCELERATING.

rituals.name: THREE-SLOT WINDOW
rituals.plain:
Only a small window stays open. Your mind isn't an endless waiting room.
Place the three most recent actionable thoughts into slots A, B, C. When a new item arrives, drop A, shift B→A and C→B, then place the new item in C.
Only three items may remain active at once.
Promote an older item only if it has a real deadline or consequence that outranks recency.

rituals.name: REHEARSAL STRESS TEST
rituals.plain:
Hold an item while doing another small job. Memory has a multitasking limit.
Hold the key claim once. Then solve two tiny unrelated tasks—such as naming two colours around you—before bringing the claim back.
Don't refresh the target while doing the intervening task.
Compare which details return automatically and which require reconstruction.

Compare exact features rather than overall familiarity.

rituals.name: CONTROL BINS

Does this thought change your next action? The unhelpful ones don't need a committee.
Take three active concerns. Sort each into CAN CHANGE NEXT or CANNOT CHANGE NEXT without solving the content.
A thought enters CAN CHANGE NEXT only if it alters a real next step.
Choose one item from the first bin for action and refuse to promote anything from the second bin during this round.

Let the original worry disappear for a moment and retrieve only the note.

rituals.name: REFRESH TAX
rituals.plain:
Refresh a different item for a moment. The loudest thought can share service.
Hold the dominant thought plus one neutral mental item. Each time the neutral item begins to fade, refresh it. Don't deliberately refresh the dominant thought.
You may refresh only one non-dominant item.
Notice whether the dominant thought still feels self-sustaining or whether it depended on your repeated returns.

rituals.name: MEMORY EDGE

From the event, retrieve one detail from the beginning, one from the middle, and one from the end.
Ease of recall is measured separately from importance.
Ask which position came easiest and whether that easy detail has been dominating the story you tell about the whole event.

rituals.name: OVERLOAD EDGE
rituals.plain:
When does one more item crowd another out? Your head has finite shelf space.
Start with two active concerns you can hold clearly. Add a third, then a fourth if manageable. After each addition, check whether an earlier item has vanished or blurred.
Add one item at a time and test retention after each addition.
Stop at the first displacement and reduce the active set by one.

rituals.name: FALSE-DILEMMA GATE
rituals.plain:
Is that really either/or? The options may be wearing fake uniforms.
Write the thought as A or B. Test four states mentally: A only, B only, both, neither.
A true exclusive choice allows exactly one side ON.
If BOTH or NEITHER is plausible, label the original frame FALSE DILEMMA.

rituals.name: THRESHOLD HALVER
rituals.plain:
At what confidence level does your choice change? The dial has a useful tipping point.
Ask whether you would act at 50% confidence. If yes, search 0–50; if no, search 50–100. Halve the remaining interval a few times.
Search by halves; don't debate every number.
Compare the discovered action threshold with the certainty level your mind has been demanding.

rituals.name: CERTAINTY BITMASK
rituals.plain:
Build confidence from separate bits. One loud feeling isn't a data set.
Imagine four support bits worth 8, 4, 2, and 1. Assign distinct evidence to bits only when it genuinely adds independent support.
Each evidence source may switch on only one bit.
Add the active bits and compare the total with the certainty your mind originally claimed.

rituals.plain:
Which rule fits the hits and the misses? The favourite example doesn't own the theory.
Recall a few situations that fit the belief and a few that did not. Look for the simplest rule that separates the two sets.
Use examples where the outcome happened and where it did not.
Test the current situation against the inferred rule rather than against the single example that came to mind first.

Do you choose differently when making a bundle? Compare the picks.
Available snacks: apple, chocolate, nuts. Round A: choose three snacks for three future days all at once. Round B: imagine choosing today's snack fresh on each of three days. Compare variety.
Use the same three available options in both rounds.
Keep the available option set unchanged across both rounds.
jolly.mindBend: People may choose more variety when several future selections are made at once than when choosing day by day.
jolly.safety: Use only harmless, low-stakes preferences. If the snack example feels personally loaded, switch to a neutral category such as music, books or routes; stop if the comparison becomes compulsive optimisation.

rituals.name: INFERENCE RESIDUE
rituals.plain:
Subtract what you observed from what you're claiming. Your story packed extra luggage.
Mentally list everything the thought says is true as set A. List only directly observed facts as set B. Remove every B item from A.
The remainder is inference, not automatically error.
Look at what remains and label it INFERENCE RESIDUE.

rituals.name: LAYER TRANSFER
rituals.plain:
Move one layer at a time. No giant story on a tiny fact.
Represent three layers: FACT, INTERPRETATION, NEXT ACTION. Move them one at a time into that order, checking that each upper layer has enough support beneath it.
FACT supports MEANING; MEANING may support ACTION; a global identity judgment can't sit directly on one fact.
If a broad self-story has no supporting middle layer, it can't be placed.

rituals.name: L-SHIFT PERSPECTIVE
rituals.plain:
Try a sideways route to the viewpoint. Your usual road isn't the only road.
Choose two axes, such as TIME and PERSON. Move two steps on the first—today to one month from now—and one step on the second—you to a neutral observer.
Change two dimensions in one direction and one in another.
Ask the same question from that new coordinate without returning through the intermediate viewpoints.

Count the differences without deciding which version is emotionally stronger.

rituals.name: PATH WEIGHT

Start with two broad future branches. Create the next layer by combining neighbouring assumptions into possible outcomes, then one more layer if useful.
More mental routes to a scenario don't automatically mean more real-world probability.
Notice which middle outcome receives the most imagined paths and ask whether it has more evidence or merely more routes.

rituals.name: FORECAST ANGLE
rituals.plain:
How far does the forecast point from the facts? Certainty may need a compass.
Imagine a clock. Point one hand toward the direction suggested by current facts and the other toward where the thought predicts things are heading.
One hand follows what the facts currently indicate; the other follows the prediction.
Estimate whether the angle is small, medium, or nearly opposite and ask what evidence would be needed to close it.

rituals.name: SOUND INTERFERENCE
rituals.plain:
Similar sounds may crowd each other in memory. Your inner rehearsal has noisy neighbours.
Hold the thought's key phrase briefly. Insert a harmless sound-similar word for a beat, then later a clearly different-sounding word.
The neutral items must differ in sound similarity, not meaning.
Compare which interruption makes the original wording harder to replay exactly.

Put NOW between past and future. Time can hold up both hands.
Build five slots: PAST-2 / PAST-1 / NOW / FUTURE-1 / FUTURE-2. Put the relevant memory and prediction pieces into matching positions.
Positions equally distant from NOW must be compared.
Check whether the future slots are merely mirrored versions of the past slots rather than independently supported forecasts.

rituals.name: REPRESENTATIONAL MOMENTUM
rituals.plain:
Freeze the imagined motion. Your mind is leaning into the next frame.
Imagine a dot moving steadily left to right across a line. Stop it exactly at the centre. Immediately mark where the dot seems as if it should be next.
The object physically stops at the marked endpoint.
Compare the expected continuation point with the actual stop point.

rituals.name: STORY PERMUTATIONS
rituals.plain:
Three facts, several orders. Your favourite story is one seating plan.
Choose three concrete facts from the situation. Mentally run all six possible orders in which they could be arranged.
Facts stay identical; only order changes.
Notice how many different stories can be generated without adding a single new fact.

rituals.name: GO / NO-GO
rituals.plain:
GO only when the rule says GO. Enthusiasm isn't the rulebook.
Run this sequence once: DOG, TABLE, CAT, CLOUD, HORSE, SPOON. Internally say TAP only on the animal items.
Say TAP internally for animals; do nothing for non-animals.
A correct NO-GO is silent; don't replace it with another response.

rituals.name: NO-CARRY WORRY

Work, relationship, health, money, and self-worth stay in their own columns unless a real link exists.
Find any 'carry' where one problem is being used as evidence that another problem is worse.

rituals.name: LOOP COMPRESSION
rituals.plain:
Repeated thought, repeated thought, repeated thought. The echo can stop sending full invoices.
Watch the thought for repeated operations such as CHECK, WHY, REPLAY, PREDICT. When the same operation repeats, code it as 3×CHECK or 4×WHY instead of following every copy.
Consecutive repeats become one item plus a count.
Reconstruct the original loop from the code and notice how much of its apparent length came from duplication.

Watch the thought for repeated operations such as CHECK, WHY, REPLAY, PREDICT. When the same operation repeats, code it as 3×CHECK or 4×WHY instead of following every copy.
Consecutive repeats become one item plus a count.
Reconstruct the original loop from the code and notice how much of its apparent length came from duplication.
cheeky.mindBend: Compression exposes the difference between how long a loop lasts and how much information it contains.
cheeky.safety: Keep this to a low-stakes mental game for one pass. When self-judgment from frustration develops, leave the exercise; switch to an ordinary activity.
